title: How many Major Atlantic Hurricanes will occur in the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season?
resolution_criteria: This question will resolve as the number of major Atlantic hurricanes that occur between June 1, 2026, and November 30, 2026, inclusive, as reported by the [National Hurricane Center (NHC)](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/?atlc) of the United States National Weather Service on December 1, 2026.
fine_print: The question will be resolved using storm reports and data published by the National Hurricane Center as of December 1, 2026. Any subsequent revisions upgrading or downgrading a storm's intensity will not be considered. The NHC [Tropical Cyclone Advisory Archive](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/2024/) and [Monthly Atlantic Tropical Weather Summary](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/text/MIATWSAT.shtml) may be used.
background:
The Atlantic hurricane season runs from June 1 to November 30, with peak activity occurring in August, September, and October. Major hurricanes, classified as Category 3 or higher on the [Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/aboutsshws.php), have sustained wind speeds of at least 111 miles per hour (178 km/h) and can cause significant damage and loss of life.

As of August 2026, no major hurricanes have taken place during the 2026 season, with only 4 named storms and a total [accumulated cyclone energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accumulated_cyclone_energy) of only 3.2.

On August 6, [NOAA released](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/outlooks/hurricane.shtml) a forecast of a 70% probability for the following ranges:

* 7-13 Named Storms, including the 2 named storms that had been recorded to that point
* 2-6 Hurricanes
* 0-2 Major Hurricanes
* Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE) range of 30-90% of the median, including the 3% that had been recorded to that point

If fewer than 2 Major Hurricanes occur, it would be the fewest since 2013.

comments.author: hamish
comments.text: First forecast on Metaculus — mostly getting a feel for the app and how forecasting works. Reasoning: one major hurricane appears to have already formed, so 0 is near impossible. With roughly seven weeks left in an El Niño season that’s past its peak, I think another major is unlikely but not rare — late-season majors have happened before (e.g. Wilma 2005, Michael 2018). Sitting slightly above the crowd on 2+ to allow for that. Haven’t checked the NHC outlook yet; will update if anything develops.

comments.author: Vlad25
comments.text:
Last year the Atlantic saw 4 major hurricanes (category 3 or higher) with 3 reaching category 5. This was determined to be a particularly intense season. The main causes of such an intense hurricane season are sea surface temperatures as well as wind shear-lower wind shears favour stronger storms. 

As well as this El Nino and La Nina both affect Atlantic wind shear whilst La Nina favours more Atlantic hurricane activity, El Nino suppresses them. In 2026 El Nino has increased wind shear and supressed hurricane development, therefore with the short window of time my prediction will be that having more than one will be highly unlikely.

comments.author: VectorWright
comments.text:
Isaias already answered the "will there be at least one" question, mostly. It peaked as a Cat 3 in the Gulf before weakening to Cat 2 at landfall near Destin on the Florida Panhandle. eylonbsh's comment below is the one thing that could move this: NHC's operational Cat 3 call on Isaias could still get revised down in post-storm best-track analysis before the Dec 1 resolution cutoff. So "0" isn't fully dead, just very unlikely now, maybe 1%.



The rest of the season has been suppressed enough that a second major breaking through looks unlikely too. Just 7 named storms and one hurricane total through early October. The reason is a historically strong El Nino, with multiple outlets putting it at 75-90%+ odds of becoming one of the strongest since 1950, and it's still strengthening heading into Q4. Strong El Nino means more sinking air and more wind shear over the Atlantic basin, which is exactly what kills storms before they reach Cat 3+.



November is also a structurally quiet month for major hurricanes even in a normal year, so the window left is short and climatologically unfavorable on top of that. Landing close to the existing community numbers: roughly 1% on 0 (downgrade risk), 88% on exactly 1, 10% on 2, and under 1% combined on 3 or more.

comments.author: eylonbsh
comments.text: 1: 87%, 2: 10.5%. Isaias reached 105 kt (Cat 3) on Oct 9, so the count is already 1. Another major before Nov 30 is unlikely: El Nino season with a record-late first hurricane, and climatology gives \~0.3-0.5 majors after mid-October in average years (fewer in El Nino years), so \~10-12% for one or more additional. Small 1% on 0 for a downgrade of Isaias.

comments.author: MaxA
comments.text: @(exmateriae) It's also late in the season when majors are historically less likely, El Nino or not. So the time decay is stronger even though we still have 7 weeks.

comments.author: exmateriae
comments.text: I think the community shouldn't be so high on 1 now that we've seen El Nino is not powerful enough to stop this from happening. Sure odds are decreasing each day but there's still almost two months.

comments.author: sai_39
comments.text: At the [latest full NHC advisory](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/mobile/text/refresh/MIATCPAT4%2Bhtml/090857.shtml), Isaias is already at 95 kt / 110 mph with a central pressure of 963 mb. Category 3 begins at 111 mph/96 kt, although NHC operational intensity estimates are normally given in 5-kt increments, so practically we're waiting for an upgrade to \~100 kt.
